> While the core API provides the fundamental data structures and
> transformations, MLFs operate across this hierarchy to deliver tasks
> such as classification, clustering, similarity search, or other
> model‑driven analyses. They do not replace the core API; instead, they
> orchestrate and combine its primitives into reusable, semantically
> richer workflows that simplify advanced processing and make complex
> analytical patterns easier to express.

``` python
from fhemb.utils.cutils import prepare_data, split_scale_data
```

## Prepare Data

``` python

def prepare_data(
    X0:ndarray, # Time series data for class 0 of shape (n_samples_0, n_timesteps, n_features) or (n_samples_0, n_timesteps).
    X1:ndarray, # Time series data for class 1 of shape (n_samples_1, n_timesteps, n_features) or (n_samples_1, n_timesteps).
)->tuple: # X: Concatenated and cleaned time series of shape (n_balanced_samples, n_timesteps, n_features).
y: Class labels (0 or 1) of shape (n_balanced_samples,).

```

*Prepare multi-class time series data for machine learning.* Performs
data cleaning, deduplication, NaN removal, and class balancing on two
sets of time series data representing different classes.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Split and Scale Data

``` python

def split_scale_data(
    X:ndarray, # Time series of shape (n_samples, n_timesteps, n_features).
    y:ndarray, # Labels of shape (n_samples,).
    test_size:float=0.3, # Fraction of samples for test split.
    random_state:int=42, # Seed for stratified split.
    normalize:NoneType=None, # None, 'minmax', 'meanvar', or fitted scaler
): # (X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test, scaler)

```

*Stratified train-test split with optional normalization.*

`normalize` may be:

    - None: no scaling
    - 'minmax': fit MinMax scaler on train, apply to test
    - 'meanvar': fit MeanVariance scaler on train, apply to test
    - fitted scaler instance: reuse without refitting

## Train and Test Classifiers

``` python
from fhemb.utils.cutils import calc_similarity, calc_accuracies
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Calculate accuracy or f1 score

``` python

def calc_similarity(
    y_test:ndarray, # Ground truth labels of shape (n_samples,).
    y_pred:ndarray, # Predicted labels of shape (n_samples,).
    sim_metric:str='accuracy', # Similarity metric to use. Options: 'accuracy', 'f1'. Default: 'accuracy'.
)->float: # Computed similarity score between 0 and 1.

```

*Calculate a similarity metric between test labels and predictions.*

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Train, test, and evaluate multiple classifiers

``` python

def calc_accuracies(
    X_train:matrix, # Training feature matrix of shape (n_samples_train, n_features).
    X_test:matrix, # Test feature matrix of shape (n_samples_test, n_features).
    y_train:ndarray, # Training labels of shape (n_samples_train,).
    y_test:ndarray, # Test labels of shape (n_samples_test,).
)->dict: # Dictionary mapping classifier names to accuracy scores.
Keys are formatted as 'classifier_variant' (e.g., 'knn_euclidean', 'svm_rbf', 'rotf').
Values are float accuracies between 0 and 1.

```

*Compute classification accuracies across multiple classifier
algorithms.*

Tests multiple supervised learning algorithms (SVM, KNN, Random Forest,
etc.) on the provided train-test data and returns accuracies for each
classifier-metric combination.

#### Classifier Variant Naming Convention

The return value is a dictionary mapping **classifier variants** to
accuracy scores.

Each key is constructed as: `<classifier_name>_`

where:

- KNN expands over **distance metrics**
- SVM expands over **kernel types**
- Other classifiers have a **single variant** (no suffix)

>

> <tbody>
> <tr>
> <td><code>euclidean</code></td>
> <td>Standard L2 distance</td>
> <td><span class="math inline">$d(x,y) = \sqrt{\sum_i (x_i -
> y_i)^2}$</span></td>
> <td>Raw feature vectors</td>
> <td>Stable, widely used, works well with normalized data</td>
> <td>Equivalent to Minkowski with <span
> class="math inline"><em>p</em> = 2</span></td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><code>nan_euclidean</code></td>
> <td>NaN‑aware Euclidean distance</td>
> <td>Same as Euclidean, computed only over non‑NaN dimensions</td>
> <td>Raw features with possible NaNs</td>
> <td>Robust when some features are missing</td>
> <td>Ignores NaN dimensions; rescales by observed dims</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><code>minkowski</code></td>
> <td>Generalized Lp distance</td>
> <td><span
> class="math inline"><em>d</em>(<em>x</em>, <em>y</em>) = (∑<sub><em>i</em></sub>∥<em>x</em><sub><em>i</em></sub> − <em>y</em><sub><em>i</em></sub>∥<sup><em>p</em></sup>)<sup>1/<em>p</em></sup></span></td>
> <td>Raw features; requires <code>p</code></td>
> <td>Flexible family including L1, L2, L∞</td>
> <td><code>p</code> passed via
> <code>calc_knn_similarity(p=...)</code></td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><code>cosine</code></td>
> <td>Cosine distance (1 − cosine similarity)</td>
> <td><span class="math inline">$d(x,y) = 1 - \frac{x \cdot
> y}{\|x\|\|y\|}$</span></td>
> <td>Raw feature vectors</td>
> <td>Good for directional / high‑dimensional data</td>
> <td>Scale‑invariant; undefined for zero vectors</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><code>l1</code></td>
> <td>Manhattan (cityblock) distance</td>
> <td><span
> class="math inline"><em>d</em>(<em>x</em>, <em>y</em>) = ∑<sub><em>i</em></sub>∥<em>x</em><sub><em>i</em></sub> − <em>y</em><sub><em>i</em></sub>∥</span></td>
> <td>Raw feature vectors</td>
> <td>Robust to outliers; sparse‑friendly</td>
> <td>Equivalent to Minkowski with <span
> class="math inline"><em>p</em> = 1</span></td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><code>precomputed</code></td>
> <td>User‑supplied distance matrix</td>
> <td><em>No equation — distances provided externally</em></td>
> <td>Requires full distance matrices for train/test</td>
> <td>Allows DTW, soft‑DTW, custom metrics</td>
> <td><code>X_train</code> and <code>X_test</code> must be distance
> matrices</td>
> </tr>
> </tbody>
> </table>

## Diagnose via Dimensionality Reduction

<div>

> **Projection into a low-dimensional space**
>
> is based on **dimensionality reduction methods**: `MDS` and `TSNE`
> from `sklearn.manifold`, `PCA` from `sklearn.decomposition`, and
> `UMAP` from `umap-learn`.
>
> - *MDS* and *t‑SNE* internally operate on pairwise distances derived
>   from the input samples, so they can be applied directly to
>   distance‑based representations (e.g., *DTW distance matrices*).
> - *UMAP* can also consume **precomputed distances**, and unlike
>   *t‑SNE* it attempts to preserve both local neighborhoods and
>   larger‑scale manifold structure, making it well‑suited for nonlinear
>   latent spaces derived from alignment metrics.
> - *PCA*, in contrast, assumes a similarity (covariance /
>   inner‑product) structure. When the latent representation is defined
>   only through distances or alignment scores, a
>   **distance‑to‑similarity transformation** must be applied before
>   *PCA* can be used.

</div>

<div>

> **Dimensionality Reduction – Summary Table**
>
> <table>
> <colgroup>
> <col style="width: 10%" />
> <col style="width: 16%" />

> <thead>
> <tr>
> <th>Projection method</th>
> <th>Input Type</th>
> <th>What It Optimizes</th>
> <th>Strengths</th>
> <th>Weaknesses</th>
> <th>Typical Use</th>
> </tr>
> </thead>
> <tbody>
> <tr>
> <td><strong>MDS (Multidimensional Scaling)</strong></td>
> <td>Distance matrix (precomputed)</td>
> <td>Preserves pairwise distances</td>
> <td>Stable, interpretable, works directly on distances</td>
> <td>Can struggle with nonlinear structure</td>
> <td>Visualizing global geometry of distance-based data</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><strong>t‑SNE</strong></td>
> <td>Distance matrix (precomputed)</td>
> <td>Preserves local neighborhoods</td>
> <td>Excellent for clusters and nonlinear manifolds</td>
> <td>Distorts global structure; parameter‑sensitive</td>
> <td>Exploring clusters and local structure</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><strong>PCA</strong></td>
> <td>Feature matrix (or similarity derived from distances)</td>
> <td>Maximizes variance along orthogonal axes</td>
> <td>Fast, deterministic, widely understood</td>
> <td>Linear only; not naturally distance‑based</td>
> <td>Baseline dimensionality reduction and comparison</td>
> </tr>
> <tr>
> <td><strong>UMAP</strong></td>
> <td>Distance matrix (precomputed) or feature matrix</td>
> <td>Preserves local structure while retaining more global geometry</td>
> <td>Fast, scalable, manifold‑aware; good balance of local/global
> structure</td>
> <td>Sensitive to <code>n_neighbors</code> and <code>min_dist</code>;
> axes not interpretable</td>
> <td>General‑purpose embedding for nonlinear structure with better global
> faithfulness</td>
> </tr>
> </tbody>
> </table>
